claims.text: The magnetocaloric response and hysteresis are primarily governed by grain-boundary density and associated interfacial strain.
Grain-boundary density and interfacial strain strongly influence coupling between the magnetic and structural transitions.
The as-deposited alloy is a relatively coarse-grained, ordered, single-phase hexagonal material.
The as-deposited alloy exhibits a strongly coupled first-order magnetostructural transition.
The as-deposited alloy has pronounced thermal and magnetic hysteresis.
Controlled high-energy ball milling can reduce the grain size to approximately 20–100 nm.
Grain refinement increases grain-boundary density and surface-to-volume ratio.
Ball milling can modify and relax the internal stress distribution without changing the alloy composition or hexagonal phase.
Increased grain-boundary area together with reduced internal strain eases nucleation and propagation of the magnetostructural transition.
Reduced internal stress and elastic constraint lower the transition energy barriers.
Lower transition barriers enable more homogeneous nucleation of the structural transformation.
Nanostructuring will reduce the latent heat associated with the first-order transition.
Nanostructuring will reduce the hysteresis width during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Nanostructuring will broaden the magnetocaloric response.
Nanostructuring will cause a modest decrease in peak magnetic entropy change while retaining a sizable response.
The increased surface-to-volume ratio will improve heat exchange and magnetic-cooling cycle efficiency.
The predicted benefits should hold for grain sizes of approximately 20–100 nm if the single-phase hexagonal structure remains intact.
The predicted benefits should be observable at applied fields of a few tesla near the intrinsic magnetostructural transition temperature.
Outside the specified grain-size, phase, field, or temperature regimes, hysteresis may not decrease or the magnetocaloric effect may be excessively weakened.
Defects introduced by nanostructuring may compromise mechanical stability or long-term transition reversibility.
